title: Multi-LLM Adaptive Conformal Inference for Reliable LLM Response
one_liner: Instead of throwing out true claims to be overly safe, use multiple LLMs to spot which claims are actually factual, then give a guarantee that holds for different groups.
lead: When an LLM answers a medical or legal question, you need to know which answers to trust. The challenge: if you reject claims too cautiously, you discard real facts. If you reject too loosely, unsafe claims slip through. MACI solves this by multiplying together confidence scores from multiple LLMs and carefully guaranteeing that users see a predictable amount of correct claims, even when different groups of people ask.

problem.h2: The two traps of factuality checking
paras: An LLM can confidently output false information. In medicine or law, a wrong answer causes real harm. So you need a guardrail: a threshold below which you refuse the LLM's claim.

But here is the trap: if you set the threshold conservatively, you reject too many true claims along with the false ones. If you set it loosely, you let dangerous false claims through. And the problem gets worse when you look at subgroups: a threshold that works for medical claims might fail for legal ones, or work for expert questions but fail for layperson ones.

Naive approaches use simple linear models or fixed rules to decide what to reject. These are too rigid to capture the messy reality that some domains, question types, or user groups have different patterns of what is true.

callout.html: You need a way to reject false claims without losing true ones, and guarantee it works fairly across different groups.

panels.title: 1. The LLM answers
panels.caption: LLM generates a claim. Is it true or false?

panels.title: 2. Single scorer is stuck
panels.caption: One model's confidence is hard to calibrate safely.

panels.title: 3. Ensemble multiplies scores
panels.caption: Three LLMs each score the claim. Multiply to find the true signal.

panels.title: 4. Group calibration tunes per group
panels.caption: Adjust thresholds per domain so each sees fair accuracy.

panels.title: 5. Guarantee holds
panels.caption: Output meets promised coverage rate across all groups.

steps.text: Feed the claim to multiple LLMs and ask each for a factuality score.
Instead of averaging, multiply them; this emphasizes claims all models agree on.
For each group (e.g., medical vs. legal), find the threshold that gives the right coverage rate.
If the multiplied score exceeds the group threshold, accept the claim; otherwise reject.
The coverage (fraction of true claims retained) holds mathematically for each group.

paras: The paper shifts from a single LLM judge or a simple linear model to a multiplicative product of ensemble scores. It also shifts from a global reject threshold to a per-group threshold that is tuned so each group sees the promised coverage rate.

hidden.h2: Coverage rate: the guarantee that actually holds
hidden.name: Coverage rate per group
paras: Coverage is the fraction of true claims your system accepts. If you promise 95% coverage, you mean: of all the true claims, your system keeps 95% and rejects only 5%. This is a distribution-free guarantee—it holds regardless of where the claims come from or what the LLM learned, because it is defined purely from observed data.

The paper estimates coverage by measuring: on a validation set from each group, what fraction of the claims flagged as true by humans does the multiplied score accept? Then it tunes the threshold for that group until the coverage hits the target.

heat.caption: Darker means higher ensemble score. Groups with different patterns need different thresholds.

reads.html: Coverage rate is how many correct claims you actually keep after filtering.
Conditional coverage: for each group g, the fraction of true claims in g that the method accepts, guaranteed to meet the target.

mechanism.h2: Why multiplying scores works better than averaging
paras: Each LLM gives a score between 0 and 1 for factuality. If you average three scores of 0.8, 0.8, and 0.6, you get 0.73. If you multiply them instead, the result is much lower (roughly 0.38). Why multiply?

Multiplication is stricter. It says: a claim is strong only if all three models agree it is strong. If one model is skeptical, the product drops dramatically, signaling that consensus is weak. Averaging would hide that disagreement. For safety in high-stakes domains, you want to catch weak consensus and reject it.

Group-conditional calibration then does the hard work: for medical claims, you may find the right threshold is 0.5 (stricter, because medicine is high-stakes); for casual queries, 0.3 suffices (looser, because the cost of rejection is lower). The paper's guarantee is that once these thresholds are set on a validation set, they hold on future data from the same groups.

math.words: The product of ensemble scores is compared to a group-specific threshold. A claim is accepted if the product exceeds the threshold and the group meets its coverage guarantee.
math.equation: accept if: score_A * score_B * score_C >= tau_g, where score_i is LLM-i factuality score, tau_g is the threshold for group g, chosen so coverage_g = target_coverage
symbols: factuality score from LLM A, between 0 and 1
factuality score from LLM B, between 0 and 1
factuality score from LLM C, between 0 and 1
rejection threshold for group g, tuned to achieve target coverage
user-specified fraction of true claims to retain (e.g., 0.95)
actual fraction of true claims in group g that the threshold accepts

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Medical claim: LLM-A says 0.9, LLM-B says 0.85, LLM-C says 0.88. Product = 0.9 * 0.85 * 0.88 = 0.673.
Medical group threshold tau_med = 0.60 (tuned so 95% of true medical claims are accepted).
Legal claim: LLM-A says 0.7, LLM-B says 0.65, LLM-C says 0.75. Product = 0.7 * 0.65 * 0.75 = 0.341.
Legal group threshold tau_law = 0.50 (tuned so 95% of true legal claims are accepted).
Since 0.341 < 0.50, the claim is rejected (LLM consensus too weak for this high-stakes domain).

math.note: Multiplying emphasizes consensus among the three LLMs; stricter thresholds per group ensure safety where the cost of error is high.

charts.title: Simple linear model (baseline)
charts.note: Single global threshold cannot adjust fairly across groups. Medicine loses coverage, law loses coverage, but false claims still slip through.

charts.title: MACI (this paper)
charts.note: Group-specific thresholds keep coverage high and false-claim rate low for each domain, with a distribution-free guarantee.

items.html: If all three LLMs are trained the same way, multiplying their scores gives no new signal. You need models that have learned different facts or different ways of reasoning. If they are identical, the product is just one weak score cubed.

items.b: New group appears at test time.
items.html: The threshold tau_g was tuned on a validation set from group g. If a completely new group (e.g., a domain never seen in validation) appears, the guarantee no longer holds. You must retune on that group first.
If the validation set used to compute coverage is not representative of the real group (e.g., simpler claims than users will ask), the threshold will be too loose or too strict in the field.
Use diverse models (different base LLMs or fine-tuning runs), validate on data truly representative of each group, and retune thresholds when new groups emerge.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a system with three LLMs (or multiple prompting variants of one model that behave differently). Collect a validation set of 100 claims from two domains (e.g., medical trivia and movie facts). Have humans label each as true or false. Compute the ensemble product score for each. For each domain, find the threshold that achieves exactly 90% coverage on that domain's validation data. Then test the thresholds on a held-out test set and report: (1) coverage per domain on the test set, (2) false-claim rejection rate, (3) number of claims accepted vs. rejected.
demo.metric_eq: coverage_medical_test = (# true medical claims accepted) / (# true medical claims in test), similarly for other groups. false_claim_rate = (# false claims accepted) / (# false claims in test).
demo.closing: The demo proves that group-specific thresholds keep coverage close to the target (90%) in each domain without sacrificing the rejection of false claims.
